thread.document:
Group Members: Akhil Agarwal, Nikhil Mathihalli, Tyler Pham, Aryan Bansal

Our Website: https://cs182-ec-a.vercel.app/

Our Code: https://github.com/Akhil-Agarwal-123/cs182-ec-a 

We wanted our website to be streamlined and intuitive, while also providing key information about everything we found while going through the analysis!

Features

Overview Page

On this page, there is a simple matrix showing how many posts were made related to each of the LLM-homework pairs. You can click on entries in the matrix to automatically get taken to the post page with the corresponding filters selected (see below for description of this page). There's also a bar graph to sum up the number of posts about each LLM.

Post Page

On this page, you can see a list of all of the posts, with the ability to show attachments embedded in the website, and it copies the formatting from Ed (including bolding etc). It also allows users to click to be taken to the post directly on Ed. We also added a filtering section, where users can select between the homeworks and the LLMs, and also search by author/title/content.

Analysis Page

This is where the main analysis happens. We allow users to add different columns for the LLMs they want to analyze, and they'll show up side by side for comparison. They can also filter by all homeworks / a specific homework. We conducted our own summarizing analysis for each post, each LLM-homework pair which had a post about it, and also had insights for each LLM as a whole (aggregated across all homeworks), so it displays these along with the posts with the same abilities to embed attachments, show formatted posts, and open in Ed.

Findings

We also had a few findings while making this – first off, we wrote our own API calling script to get the data we needed from the posts, since there's no official API, and the unofficial ones we found were just listening to new events, not scraping existing courses.

We also found that almost everyone followed the same format / had some specific keywords in their post titles to identify as special participation A, and also say which homework & llm they used, but for the rest, we were able to get the information from the contents of the post, without needing any LLM! This saved a lot of time from having to pass all these posts into LLMs.

Next, for the actual website, Gemini Pro was able to one-shot a decent amount of the website, but there were still a LOT of bugs. While we were able to get some of them fixed by Gemini, some others (some of which were very simple, such as getting the divs not to expand past or be smaller than the window width), were not able to be fixed, and so we did this ourselves (take that, vibe coding :) ). There were lots of theme bugs as well, with a lot of elements showing up as completely black, and we had to refactor the code and fix that ourselves as well.

Also, in terms of design choices, we made sure to allow this entire pipeline to be replicated given an Ed API key and replacing the course ID, since there was no manual filtering done at any point, and it's all code.

comments.content: <document version="2.0"><paragraph>This is very cool! Really like how clean the first page is. Is it possible to move 'unknown' to the bottom, and have the LLM list the top 5-6 models and have the others move into an 'other' category or perhaps expand on click? </paragraph><paragraph/><paragraph/><paragraph>Especially like the the comparison. Right now it is a bit hard to understand the compare mode since it feels like info overload. But could you compare two different models on the same HW and see how they were different --- with precise annotations? The AI generated summary differences are hard to get anything out of.  That might be a nicer way to present it. </paragraph><paragraph/><paragraph>I'm wondering if there is a way to make a mini-LLM arena out of this. <break/></paragraph><paragraph>None of this is required but are nice to have features to make the website more useable. </paragraph></document>
